learn.title: Two classic examples
learn.body: The factorial of n, written n!, is n times every whole number below it down to 1. So 5! is 5 times 4 times 3 times 2 times 1, which is 120. It has a neat recursive form: n! equals n times (n - 1)!, and 1! is 1.

learn.title: Factorial
learn.body: We use `long long` because factorials grow very fast.

learn.title: Watch the size
learn.body: 12! is 479,001,600, which fits in a 32-bit int. 13! is 6,227,020,800, which does not. A `long long` holds up to 20!, and 21! overflows even that. Overflow of signed integers is undefined behaviour in C, so avoid it.

learn.title: Fibonacci numbers
learn.body: The Fibonacci sequence goes 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13. Each number is the sum of the two before it. Recursively: `fib(n)` is `fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)`, with two base cases, `fib(0)` is 0 and `fib(1)` is 1.

learn.title: Fibonacci
learn.body: The function calls itself twice, so each call branches into two more.

learn.title: Calls in fib(4)
steps: `fib(2)` is computed twice, and so are some others
In total `fib(4)` makes 9 calls, and `fib(10)` makes 177

questions.prompt: What are the base cases of `fib`?
questions.explanation: Both 0 and 1 return their own value, and every larger call reduces toward them.
fib(5) is 5 and fib(4) is 3, so fib(6) is 5 + 3 = 8.
n! is n times the factorial of the next smaller number.

choices: Factorials get too big for an int quickly

questions.prompt: How many calls does `fib(5)` make, counting itself?
questions.explanation: fib(5) makes 1 call for itself, 9 for fib(4) and 5 for fib(3): 15 calls in all.
